newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. showing renewed interest in Africa - UNDP.
newsitem.headline: U.S. showing renewed interest in Africa - UNDP.

text.p: Donors are reducing development aid to the world's poorest countries at a time when the rich are getting richer, but the United States is showing renewed interest in Africa, a senior United Nations official said on Wednesday.

U.N. Development Programme (UNDP) administrator James Gustave Speth said development aid to the world's poor had slumped by 20 percent since 1992 and appealed to donor states to relax purse strings to reverse the decline.

Official development aid is now at an all-time low of an average 0.27 percent of Gross Domestic Product in the industrialised nations of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), Speth told a news conference.

"It's ironic that at a time when the needs of the developing world are increasing dramatically...we find that the resources to do this job have declined by 20 percent. We need to reverse this tragic decline," he said.
UNDP operates in 150 countries and spent $2.2 billion in 1996. About half its programmes were in Africa, Speth said.
He later told Reuters that he expected the United States to buck the global fall in development aid, particularly in Africa.
"Africa remains a very high priority for us and for the United States," Speth said.

"The situation in the United States is at a turning point, I think. It does look like some of the opposition to development assistance is beginning to moderate and support for development assistance in the U.S. is beginning to pick up.

"We at the UNDP hope to regain a lot of the loss that we took when the U.S. cut our support in 1996. In 1998, we hope to recover fully from that cut. I hope it will begin an upturn in the United States. There seems to be a deepening and widening concern with the situation in Africa."

Washington has shown a sudden interest this year in the world's poorest continent where French policy over how to keep exclusive control over Francophone Africa remains in disarray and Britain is showing little interest in its former colonies.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has launched a new Africa investment initiative, and on Tuesday he announced a trade and economic development plan for the continent.

In Rwanda, the United States has replaced France as a key military and political ally. The United States has also been supportive of former rebels who swept to power in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo (formerly Zaire), where U.S. firms have begun to make inroads to exploit mineral riches after years of European domination in Africa's largest French-speaking country.
